summary: Examines address resolution problems that appear when data centers grow to very large numbers of hosts. It focuses on ARP for IPv4 and Neighbor Discovery for IPv6, and describes the scaling issues they can cause. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Computers use address resolution to find the link-layer address for an IP address. This RFC explains why that process can become a burden in data centers with many hosts and virtual machines.

subtitle: Address-resolution scaling problems in large data centers

tldr.problem: Large Layer 2 data-center networks can create substantial ARP and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery traffic. Virtual machines and workload movement can increase pressure to keep Layer 2 domains large.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes IPv4 and IPv6 address resolution, common data-center topologies and load points on routers and switches.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational problem statement that itemizes pain points and proposes no solutions.

sections.title: Address Resolution at Data-Center Scale
sections.content:
Address resolution finds the link-layer address associated with an IP address. IPv4 uses ARP and IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery (ND). Although resolution is limited to a Layer 2 broadcast domain, many interfaces and VLANs can spread the work across routers, switches and links.

The RFC focuses on address-resolution problems in large data centers. It records current pain points rather than proposing a fix or addressing every data-center scaling issue.
sections.plainLanguage: A network device needs a link-layer address before it can send a packet on a local link. This RFC looks at how that lookup process behaves when a data center has many devices.

sections.title: Why Layer 2 Domains Grow
sections.content:
As a Layer 2 broadcast domain grows, it carries more broadcast traffic, including ARP requests that switches, hosts and routers may need to process. Large amounts of broadcast traffic can contribute to broadcast storms. One conventional approach is to split a data center into smaller Layer 2 networks, such as one subnet per rack.

That approach can make it harder to move a virtual machine between racks without changing its IP address. Virtualization lets one physical server host many virtual machines, each with its own IP and MAC address, and increases pressure for flexible workload placement. The RFC cites data centers with over 100,000 physical machines.
sections.plainLanguage: Smaller local networks can limit broadcast traffic, but moving a virtual machine between them may require an address change. Larger networks make movement easier while increasing address-resolution work.

sections.title: ARP and IPv6 Neighbor Discovery
sections.content:
ARP sends a broadcast request to the Layer 2 network, and the node that owns the requested IP address replies. The RFC notes that ARP's behavior is sparsely specified and implementations vary, including in how they retransmit requests and clear stale cache entries. Some systems periodically clear caches and issue new queries.

IPv6 ND uses multicast to a solicited-node multicast address rather than broadcast. Network cards can often filter multicast queries that do not concern their host, reducing work in host software. Where that filtering is unavailable, such as in a hypervisor, the virtual switch may need to perform it.
sections.plainLanguage: ARP asks every device on a local network who owns an address. IPv6 Neighbor Discovery sends a multicast query intended for a smaller set of listeners, though software may still need to filter it.

sections.title: Where the Layer 3 Boundary Sits
sections.content:
The RFC describes a data center with access switches near servers, aggregation switches connecting access switches, and a core connecting the aggregation layer to larger networks. Where the Layer 3 boundary sits affects the size of Layer 2 domains and where address-resolution work accumulates.

Routing at access switches keeps each rack's Layer 2 domain small, but limits movement between racks without changing addresses. Routing at aggregation switches enables more VM movement but makes those switches handle more ARP and ND traffic. Keeping Layer 3 in the core allows wider Layer 2 domains and creates the largest address-resolution impact. Overlays move resolution into overlay traffic rather than eliminating it.
sections.plainLanguage: Moving the Layer 3 boundary higher allows virtual machines to move across more racks without address changes. It also makes more switches and routers handle address-resolution traffic.

sections.title: Router and Switch Pressure
sections.content:
Routers often process ARP in a software slow path, which handles fewer packets per second than forwarding hardware. The RFC describes processing capacity in the low thousands of ARP packets per second and notes that a router with many interfaces sees the aggregate load across them. Queuing packets during unresolved address lookups can add CPU work.

ND has its own scaling concerns: some implementations probe in-use neighbor entries as often as every 35 seconds. Switch MAC-address tables also grow with the Layer 2 domain, and virtual machines add separate MAC addresses. The RFC concludes that these are pain points for data-center design, not a solution specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers may have to resolve addresses in software while also keeping packets waiting. Large Layer 2 domains and many virtual machines can also increase the number of entries switches must track.
